utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you own a car at this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not have a car. I used to own a car in the period when I was working in Banja Luka for about three years. I had a Visa Citroen. I sold it when I left for Libya and after that I never owned a car. 4 Q. The priest's car that you referred to, that zastava, did you all fit in this car, the eight of you? 6 A. Well, because we did not have any belongings with us, we just got in very quickly. It was a big haste and the priest was driving and I was sitting at the front passenger seat and behind there was my mother, my wife, my daughter Valentina, Aleksandra, and the wife of the priest was also sitting there, Veselka and her daughter who was several months old. We were all very cramped. I was at the front so I did not really feel that. 13 Q. Which route did the car take out of Kozarac? 14 A. Well, since we realised, we knew, that the tank was at the entrance to the town of Kozarac, we thought that it was impossible to take that road. So we took the old Banja Luka road in the direction of Banja Luka, and we thought that we could get to the main Banja Luka/Prijedor road and continue our journey towards Banja Luka because the old road is parallel to the new one, and there are several spots where you merge. So we went along that road and after 100 metres we were stopped. 22 Q. The old road you referred to, does that run past the church? 23 A. Yes. 24 Q. If you took that road in the direction of Banja Luka, it at some stage comes close to what is called the new Banja Luka/Prijedor highway, is that right? 27 A. Yes, most of it runs parallel with that road, very close, maybe some 100 metres at some spots or maybe 50, but on many spots when you drive towards Banja Luka, the two roads merge. 2 Q. Did you try to get on to the new highway towards Banja Luka? 3 A. Yes, that was the idea. After maybe 500 metres driving in the direction of Banja Luka along the old road, you could pull into the main, into the new Prijedor/Banja Luka road. I do not recall exactly the name of that spot, but that is what people mostly did when they travelled to Banja Luka because it is closer for about one kilometre as opposed to when you go to the junction, Prijedor/Banja Luka. 10 Q. Were you able to get out of Kozarac and travel to Banja Luka on that road? 12 A. No, I was surprised because after 100 metres we were stopped, as I told you. The priest talked to the man who was standing in the middle of the road, that side road. I knew that young man who was standing there. He was holding a rifle and he had a uniform, a military uniform. It was Bahonjic and I think his name is Sead, I am not quite sure, but I knew him very well because he had a private business for production of coffee machines. So I knew him very well and he sold me the coffee machine for my cafe. He was standing there. He pointed his rifle and he said that he was under orders not to let us leave Kozarac. So I asked him once again. He first talked to the priest. He was standing some 20 metres away. So I opened the door and I asked him, I begged him, to let us leave, and I said, "I will just drive my wife and children. I will come back. If you want me to stay here, I will come back. There is no problem". He said, "No, we are under orders no one should leave Kozarac". "Who 1 ordered that?" He said, "I do not know". He did not want to 2 answer my question. So at that moment I realised that on the left side 4 there was a large group of people standing behind a shelter and 5 I said, "Well, OK. I will go to the police to ask for the 6 permission to leave Kozarac", and he said, "Well, please do 7 so". We went along the road. I do not know the exact name 9 of that street, maybe Omladinska or Pionirska. Anyway, it 10 is the street that leads to the hospital in Kozarac, the health 11 centre. At the health centre it turns left and goes to the main 12 street, Marsala Tita, which leads to Mrakovica. So we went 13 along that road, in the direction of the police station, which 14 is in the main street, Marsala Tita Street, but we did not stop 15 there because there was a huge group of people standing in front 16 of the police station and everybody was armed. We simply could 17 not stop. So I saw that many people were carrying weapons and 19 there were vehicles were passing by and you could no longer tell 20 there was any kind of order at that time. People were driving 21 both on the left and the right side of the road. It was a 22 general chaos. So we drove on in the direction of Mrakovica and 23 I remember that they tried to stop us near the village of 24 Rajkovici. I know there was a well at that spot which was some 25 kind of monument, so a soldier wearing the same uniform as the 26 previous one tried to stop us. But this one had a 27 semi-automatic rifle and he also had a hand held rocket launcher 28 fixed to his rifle. I knew that man too. It was Salkanovic. They called him "Salkan", but I do not know his real name. So he tried to stop us, but we just drove past very fast and went on in the direction of Mrakovica. So, we were travelling towards Mrakovica, via the village of Podgradje. We arrived in Gradiska and then from Gradiska we set on in the direction of Banja Luka where we arrived in the evening. I know that we drove some 150 kilometres that day. 8 Q. Just to help those listening to the evidence in this case, if I can just identify a number of those streets that you referred to? You referred to leaving the old road and going up towards the health centre in Kozarac. Is that a road that is at right angles to the old road and virtually opposite the church itself? 13 A. Yes. That road goes past the house of Marinko Konjivoda on the right side, Mirko Grahovac's house on the left side, Bestalic Meho's house, and it leads right to the entrance of the health centre in Kozarac and at triangles it turns left and merges with the main street, Marsala Tita Street. 18 Q. I do not have a photograph of that street immediately to hand, but you may remember when a witness was giving evidence, an anonymous witness, that he looked at a photograph of that street but was unable to identify it. Was that the street you were referring to? 23 A. Yes. 24 Q. The direction that you took out of Kozarac towards Mrakovica and that would have been up Marsala Tita Street and the continuation of Marsala Tita Street out of Kozarac, is that right? 27 A. Yes. Yes. Marsala Tita Street goes on and it passes the villages of Dera, Rajkovici. It goes past the youth settlement, Benkovac, and it leads to Mrakovica which is the top of the Kozara mountain. From Mrakovica, you turn left from where you can only take a macadam road and after a couple of kilometres there is an asphalt road. So the road leading from Gradiska to Banja Luka, that is the road Banja Luka/Bosanska Gradiska which we used to take when travelling to Belgrade. It is a main road. 7 Q. When you arrived at Banja Luka, where did you go to stay? 8 A. We went to my brother's place, Ljubomir's place. 9 Q. Is it right that he has an apartment in a block of flats in Banja Luka? 11 A. It was not really an apartment. It was some sort of provisional accommodation. It was not a real apartment. It was in basement and there was also -- there was only one room in that basement which served both as the kitchen and bedroom. There was also a bedroom, a sort of makeshift bathroom improvised by my brother. I know that he moved there after the earthquake in Banja Luka. 18 Q. What I had asked you about was where your brother Ljubo lived in Banja Luka, what sort of accommodation he had? 20 A. Exactly what I just described, that is where he lived, and the settlement is called Starcevica. Those were really -- it was a basement unit. 23 Q. Did you stay with your brother Ljubo or did you go to live elsewhere? 25 A. We all spent the night there. It was very late when we arrived and the priest did not have a place to go. We suggested that he stayed. It was risky. We did not know what was going to go on. We did not know what was happening on the other roads, how you could get to Sanski Most. You could get there through Mrkonic Grad. He himself did not know at the time where he was going to go, to his parents or somewhere else. So, simply, we did not know what was going on. He stayed the night and the next day he left. I later found out that he went back to Omarska. 7 Q. Did you continue to stay with your brother Ljubo or did you go to live elsewhere? 9 A. We spent several days at my brother's and throughout that time my wife and myself cleaned up another residential unit in Koste Jarica Street which was not in a very good condition. We tried to make it livable where we could move in for a longer period of time. 14 Q. I would like you now to look at some photographs, Exhibit 62A and B, please? Defence 62A and B. If those photographs actually could be put straightaway on the monitor? We see on the left-hand side a photograph of a house with a gate in front of it. Do you recognise that building? 19 A. Yes. 20 Q. What is that building? 21 A. That is a house in Koste Jarica Street in Starcevica settlement in Banja Luka where I moved my family in. 23 Q. How did you come to stay in this house? 24 A. Myself and my family and my brother had a friend, Nihad Alic -- he was a salesman like my brother -- and in the course of time we all met. He was in very -- he had a very good relationship with my brother Ljubomir and he used to come to Kozarac in earlier times quite a lot, especially -- he had offered to my brother for us to move into that house. The previous residents, that is, the owners, the woman had left, she went abroad, and her husband had died or was killed, I do not remember exactly, so Nedim had the key and they offered us to move there. The house had -- it was about 50 metres, maybe less, down the road. We met and he showed us this place. 7 Q. Which part of the house did you move into? 8 A. We moved into the basement which can be seen on the right-hand side of the photograph. 10 Q. To get to the basement where would you find it in the house? 11 A. If you look at the left-hand side photograph you can see an improvised gate there. You would turn right and go around. You would come to the entrance from the side. 14 Q. Is the house itself standing on a slope? 15 A. Yes. The front side, if you look at the left-hand side photograph, that is -- this is all flat, the yard and the path, but in the back of the house the ground slopes down on a decline, and about 50 metres down there is a little creek and it is sort of grown in, overgrown. 20 Q. Looking at the photograph D62B, which is the one on the right-hand side, what does that show? 22 A. It shows the basement which you can see on the left-hand side photograph, but it is part of the same structure, of the same building. In that period, while I was staying with my brother, I tried to clean up, make it livable. My friend, Hamdija, who was a professional in there, we first painted the kitchen and that living area, so-called, even though only the kitchen really existed, it was ready to be lived in, and the rest of the 1 structure was pretty useless. So we tried to make it usable. So I was interested in putting there my wife and my 3 mother. But, under normal circumstances, in normal conditions, 4 nobody would live there. The windows were broken on the side. 5 People had broken into the building several times while the 6 owner was abroad. That was one of the reasons why Nedim offered 7 us to move there because the very presence would deter people, 8 and there were several break-ins that were happening in that 9 area. So it was beneficial for them too. To the left from the entrance there was a large room 11 which was about half of the square area of the house. There was 12 a sofa and armoire, but everything was dirty and we kept 13 cleaning it and it had a bad stench. So I moved the family in, 14 but every time I would come we kept cleaning and cleaning out. 15 I remembered behind that living room area there was a room where 16 they had a large cooler. I -- we found a freezer. We found a 17 lot of spoiled food in there. So it gave a terrible stench. I know that throughout the time we stayed there we 19 kept cleaning it out and we never finished. There was no 20 bathroom there. I heard my wife say that the conditions were 21 good, but it is not right. Maybe they were better than what 22 they had in the village of Kozice, maybe. I know that there was 23 no bathroom in this house and the toilet was improvised. When 24 we wanted to take a bath we would go to my brother's or to our 25 friend's, to the family (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your family move into this accommodation with you or did you 27 live elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, I was staying in Banja Luka all up until we moved them in and then I went back to the Kozarac. On the right-hand side photograph on that tree you can see an iron bar, and that was a TV antennae that I put up right away so that my family could maybe watch television. At that time we had no TV, but we found the antennae so I just installed it. Later, my brother brought a TV so we could watch it. But, in general, they were bad conditions. We were embarrassed to invite anybody so that they could see where we lived. I had a lot of friends in Banja Luka but I did not invite them. They all knew that I lived very well in Kozarac, and for me it was embarrassing to be here. 12 Q. You said you arrived in Banja Luka on 3rd May. About what would the date have been that your family moved into that accommodation in Koste Jarica street? 15 A. I think it was 6th May, several days, three or four, maybe it was 7th May, but I think it was 6th. I also know well that there is also a well there to the right because nothing inside really worked. It seems to me that people -- they must have been taking baths outside. 20 Q. When they moved in on 6th or 7th May, what did you do? 21 A. On the same day I went back to Kozarac, because my cafe was still open, and the young man that I told you about, Elvir, my waiter, he knew that I was not coming. He had a key. He would open up and he knew his job. He was keeping the books, and so I just joined him and we continued. Also, we had a special relationship. He was not asking many questions where I was going, when I was coming back, and I was not very strict towards him. So we got along very well. So my presence or absence did not interfere with the work. He knew his job, even if there was -- if we ran out of beverage, he would go to Adil Jakupovic, Sefik Arnautovic, and he would take care of it. 4 Q. You had returned to Kozarac; did there come a time when you eventually left Kozarac? 6 A. Yes, I left Kozarac 23rd May '92. 7 Q. I would now like to ask you some questions about that period until 23rd May 1992. Did you visit your family in Banja Luka on occasions during that time? 10 A. Yes, I did. As I said, I trusted this young man and it was no problem for me to leave. He had the keys both to the cafe and to my house and to the garage where there were supplies of alcoholic and other beverages. I often went mostly because I always took something with me. Once we -- when we first left Kozarac, we almost took nothing with us, very few things, especially when the children's things, they had no clothes. There was nothing in Banja Luka. I also remember that I took bedding. All there was in that house, everything was really neglected, and we only had one blanket so you had to fold it underneath and over your head so that you could fall asleep. There were no conditions there. So I very often went there and took things with me. It was difficult because I did not have a vehicle. We had to find a way, a bus or a truck, or find somebody who was going. So that is how I was going there. But, mostly I would not stay there; I would go and then I would come back the same day or the next. I was not staying there. 28 Q. Your brother Ljubomir described taking a TV set and a terrier dog back to Banja Luka on your behalf. Was that right? 2 A. Yes, yes, that is right, but it was not one terrier. It was two of them. They are small dogs. Maybe they were three weeks or a month old. One he took and one we left with the family where we stayed in Banja Luka, but I had a large terrier which was their mother. 7 Q. That is all I think we need to know about it for the moment. It was just the fact of it rather than the dog family history. During this period until 23rd May, we know from evidence that on 29th April 1992 there was the takeover in Prijedor and the Crisis Staff was formed in Prijedor. I want to ask you now about this period of time from 29th April until 23rd May. Is it right that there were a series of meetings that took place between the new authorities in Prijedor and representatives from Kozarac? 16 A. Yes. 17 Q. Those meetings concerned a series of ultimata that had been given to Kozarac. Were you aware of these ultimata? 19 A. Yes, I knew, but all that started by takeover of the power. I first found out and it was a shock to me. To a degree, one could understand the takeover of power, but I was shocked when I saw that the next day some people were turned back. They could not go to work. Some said that they were turned back at Orlovci and some said, "We could not go there; there are flags hanging around town". That is the first shock. That is what shocked the population, the general population, who was not familiar with this. But then I think that the whole thing went on for much 1 longer, even before the takeover, and that the official 2 authorities in Kozarac knew about it but not the general 3 population. But, after the takeover on 29th April until 4 23rd May, there were several additional meetings and there were 5 these ultimata that were coming from the Crisis Staff in 6 Prijedor. I heard about them and I know about the ultimatums 7 that were given to the police force in Kozarac, to the regular 8 police. They were not directed to the civilians and the TO and 9 the reserve police. I heard only about the ultimatums sent by 10 the police in Prijedor to the active police force in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it right that there were a number of delegations from the 12 municipality of Kozarac, and citizens who were part of the 13 municipality met those within the Crisis Staff in Prijedor to 14 discuss the state of affairs with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not that familiar about this first period, after the 16 takeover. Later, when I joined the civic forum, I found out, 17 talking to people, that these negotiations went on for a long 18 time, and there were representatives of Local Commune of Kozarac 19 taking part and the representatives of the police force, and 20 they were talking to the people from the municipalities. But, Kemal Susic told me that these negotiations were 22 interrupted at one point, maybe about two weeks before the 23 hostilities began. He told me that they had formed a citizens' 24 forum which would be non-partisan. There may have been some 25 party members in it but, by and large, they organised and they 26 wanted to join the negotiations precisely because the 27 negotiations between the local authorities in Kozarac and in 28 Prijedor had been interrupted. So, Kemal Susic and other citizens who before that had 2 no active part in the Local Commune, they visited me and they 3 asked me if I would join the same forum. I asked them about the 4 reasons for it and they told me what was going on before. That 5 is why they wanted to come and try to help in that situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why it was that the citizens forum approached you to 7 join them and take a part in their discussions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reason was a simple one. They said, Kemal Susic explained, 9 I had contact and we talked and, first of all, they knew who my 10 father was, that he was a well-known person in the municipality 11 and they thought that I could help as his son. Also they said 12 that they would also invite Bosko Dragicevic. His son was the 13 first President of the Kozara municipality earlier, and so they 14 were talking about the possibility of creating a mutual trust. They said that they would also invite several other 16 people who were non-Muslims in Kozarac. I agreed with that but, 17 frankly speaking, at first I was not sure. I did not know about 18 the real goals of this forum. I was afraid that all people 19 would be manipulated by any which party. It was risky to get 20 involved because you did not know what was behind it. We did 21 not know what was going on at the very top. We did not know 22 about the previous negotiations. We just knew that there were 23 ultimatums, that there was something going on in that respect. So we went to Prijedor with quite a bit of -- with 25 many unknowns. We knew one thing. We wanted to quiet down the 26 situation, to improve relationships with Prijedor and Banja Luka 27 and we thought of no other things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I can tell the translators are working at great speed to keep up with you, Mr. Tadic. If you could speak a little bit slower because they are trying to interpret every word. I can tell they are moving very quickly. 4 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay, what was the date that Mr. Tadic joined the citizens' forum or civic forum? 6 MR. KAY: I will ask that question. Thank you, your Honour. [To the witness]: Can you tell us when it was you decided to join the civic forum as a result of Kemal Susic approaching you? 9 A. I think it was 10th May. In the period between 10th and 23rd May we met twice in Prijedor. I remember that the last time when we met, it was 20th May. The first meeting I do not recall exactly, but it was during that period of time. 13 Q. That is the first meeting that you would have attended that you cannot recall the date, is that right? 15 A. Yes, I cannot say if it was 11th or 12th, but it was that first meeting, and then we -- after we had an agreement, we did certain things and then another meeting followed which was on 20th May. 19 Q. In both of these meetings that took place, did you play any active role? 21 A. Yes, I did. I took Kemal Susic's invitation very seriously. Then when I saw who the other members were, I really started believing the good intentions. Those were people who were not involved in the war. They were interested in business or sports, the communal living, so these were the people with whom we lived. They were my neighbours or my brothers, the people from the centre of Kozarac, who were considered to be the natives. There was Jusuf Pasic, the doctor, Kemal Balic, Hamdija Kahrimanovic, Dragoje Pupovac from Kozarusa. Bosko Dragicevic was present at the first meeting, but then refused. Ilijaz Memic was also representing the Local Commune and then he also refused to come to the second meeting and he fled abroad with his family. He was a representative of the SDA and the Local Commune. 7 Q. At the first meeting what was discussed between the various bodies who were present and represented? What was the purpose of the meeting? 10 A. I think that first it should be explained how the meeting came about. 12 Q. If you could actually answer my question first about the purpose of the meeting? 14 A. The subject was the ultimatum that was given to the police and security situation in the area of Kozarac, the Local Commune. The Local Commune of Kozarac was part of the Prijedor municipality. The main institutions were in the city of Prijedor however you felt about it, and there was a municipal Crisis Staff that was instituted there and they had the superior authority. They took over all power. At that time the civilian government did not function the way it used to. 22 Q. The representations made by the people from the civic forum in Kozarac, were they representations and were they presented in a way that you supported and agreed with? 25 A. Well, we had arrived there because we wanted to hear about what the problem was because we did not really know what the problem was, and they told us what the problem was. It was exposed by a person whom I met there for the first time, by Simo Drljaca, a 1 new chief of the Prijedor police. He mainly had the floor 2 although the meeting was also attended by the Commander of the 3 municipal Crisis Staff, Milomir Stakic and Mico Kovacevic, who 4 was the President of the Executive Council, was also there, the 5 President of the SDS, Simo Miskovic. There were several people 6 in military uniforms which I had never seen before. But mainly the problems were the relations between 8 Kozarac police and Prijedor police, and that is why Simo Drljaca 9 had the floor most of the time. He explained everything in very 10 strict terms, and he said what the problems were and they did 11 not want to talk about that, and they said who we were 12 representing and so on. "How will you implement what we agree?" 13 and so on. The only power at that time in Kozarac, it was in 14 Memic's, Ilijaz Memic's hands. So they did not know whether 15 everything we can agree would be implemented. So I know that Simo Drljaca explained, exposed, his 17 requests. He asked that active policemen sign loyalty to the 18 new government in Prijedor, to the police chief, that insignia 19 be changed and uniforms, or otherwise people who are fully 20 employed there with the police, then they should leave the 21 police and give back the weapons. Those were his main requests, 22 requests of the Chief of Police in Prijedor, Simo Drljaca. He 23 explained his requests and he also issued some kind of 24 ultimatum. He said that it was the order of the Banja Luka 25 centre of public safety, headed by Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The delegation that you were asked to join from the civic forum 27 in Kozarac, did you have an agreed policy amongst yourselves? 28 Did you actually have any power amongst yourselves to respond or 1 to in some way comply with this ultimatum from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that precisely was the big problem. We didn’t have any 3 authority, not that I knew of. Maybe some people did have some 4 kind of instructions but they did not say anything about them. 5 There was a very serious problem because in case we should come 6 to an agreement, how could we possibly implement it? So the 7 only person who had some authority in Kozarac at that time was 8 Ilijaz Memic, also Bosko Dragicevic. Bosko Dragicevic was a 9 member of the Executive Council of the Local Commune and Ilijaz 10 Memic was a representative of the SDA. They refused to 11 co-operate. Bosko Dragicevic justified himself by being very 12 busy and Memic simply packed his things and fled abroad, so we 13 just -- we remained stranded. Anyhow, there was a possibility 14 to do something. That is why members of the forum suggested a 15 meeting of the Assembly of the citizens of Kozarac which was 16 held, and they explained to them the requests issued by the 17 Municipal Assembly in Prijedor. I did not attend that Assembly, but we agreed that we 19 should go to Prijedor once again. I think it was on 20th May 20 that we went back to Prijedor and had another meeting. The same 21 people attended the meeting, municipal Crisis Staff from 22 Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The meeting in the Assembly in Kozarac, the people's Assembly, 24 can you recollect when that took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was held after our first meeting in Prijedor. It was the 26 usual procedure, because after the meeting we managed somehow to 27 find an agreement. We agreed that the ultimatum should be 28 postponed because the Chief of Police in Prijedor, Drljaca, he 1 had said what the exact date should be to implement the 2 ultimatum. So we managed to postpone it until the next meeting 3 which took place on 20th. Our representatives told that to the 4 citizens in Kozarac, to the Assembly, and a new meeting took 5 place then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can just ask you about the Citizens Assembly in Kozarac? 7 You said that you did not attend that meeting. Can you 8 recollect what the reason was, why you were not there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be frank, I simply could not. I was not allowed. I trusted 10 people whom I went with but they were also afraid. Many of them 11 were being threatened by some individuals. They were treated as 12 some sort of traitors in case anything should be agreed. So 13 I simply could not go to that meeting. But Kemal Susic informed me about the meeting and the 15 results. He came to see me after that, and he told me nothing 16 special happened, people dominated there, the same people who 17 had attended other meetings in Prijedor, and they simply stuck 18 to their proposals. Some new people appeared, people who had 19 not lived in Kozarac before that. There was a major who came to 20 the meeting. I think that his name was Menkovic, 21 Mirsad Menkovic, and Kemal told me it was unbelievable what was going 22 on at the Assembly. Some groups insisted that the weapons 23 should not be given back and that the loyalty should not be 24 signed. There were people who were looking for a compromise. 25 Anyhow, the situation was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this stage, it was obviously well-known that it had been a 27 Serb takeover of power in Prijedor, and you referred to your 28 difficulties in being able to attend that meeting. Was that 1 because lines were being drawn now between Serbs and the Muslims 2 far clearer than they had been in the previous time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the takeover in the municipality of Prijedor did create a 4 certain animosity towards us who were living in the centre of 5 Kozarac, a certain mistrust, because it all took place quite 6 unexpectedly in Prijedor. It was a shock for everybody, because 7 the local government was in the hands of the SDA, a Muslim party 8 in Prijedor, and something like a coup had happened. Of course, 9 people no longer believed anyone. They would simply turn their 10 heads away because it was difficult to believe, to trust, 11 someone, they identified the power with someone who had done 12 something terrible. They sided us somehow with them, identified us with 14 them. So what I was trying to do, I was just trying to help, as 15 far as it was possible for me, because I was from the centre of 16 Kozarac because my parents had been living there and I thought 17 that I could do something, and it was my duty to do something. 18 But, as I say, there were many groups of people who were 19 spreading lies. I don’t know if it was all on purpose, but 20 simple people were disappointed. Power had been taken away and, on the other hand, 22 everybody was acquiring weapons in Kozarac. The weapons were 23 being openly sold and you no longer knew whom to trust. There 24 was a general feeling of insecurity, and those who were not 25 organised in some units, paramilitary units, or police units, 26 they simply turned away to their own families and they just 27 cared about that. They wanted to shelter their families and 28 that was the life, that was the situation in Kozarac until 1 May '92. There was very little communication between people at 2 that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second meeting that took place in Prijedor, can you tell us 4 what was discussed at that meeting and what the atmosphere was 5 like on the 20th May?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that meeting did bring some hope that things would be 7 solved at the level of the Kozarac Local Commune, because 8 Drljaca said, although he had already said that ultimata that 9 had been issued came from Banja Luka, from the centre of 10 security services, but he denounced that because he said at 11 the second meeting, "OK, well, you do not have to change 12 insignia but you have to sign loyalty". So there was some kind of progress and we said, "Well, 14 OK, when it comes to insignia, then the police in Kozarac don’t 15 have to wear hats either". So you had a possibility of putting 16 the insignia on other parts of the uniform. But, anyhow, we 17 managed to obtain for those insignia not to be changed. But 18 there was a compromise because hats were no longer worn. That 19 was some kind of progress. But the municipal staff, there was always someone -- 21 there was a representative of the military who mentioned the 22 problem of paramilitary units in Kozarac, because in the 23 area of Kozarac there had been several incidents, mostly on the 24 Prijedor/Banja Luka road. People would stop columns of soldiers 25 that were coming back from the front in Croatia, and sometimes a 26 Serbian reserve soldier would be arrested by a group of, I do 27 not know, Suljo Kosuran or someone else, and they would be 28 detained. So it was very unsafe to walk around Kozarac for 1 everyone, everybody who belonged to either the JNA or the 2 Krajina army. So, as I say, some steps had been made, but the 4 problem was the signing of loyalty. Drljaca did say that if the 5 chief of the Banja Luka police allows, then loyalty would not 6 have to be signed. So those were the discussions that we had, 7 and we wanted to go to Banja Luka around 20th, 21st May, in 8 order to reach any kind of agreement. So, aside from that 9 ultimatum, there was an agreement also that people who were not 10 allowed to carry weapons and who were walking around with 11 weapons had to store their weapons at home. So there was a kind of agreement but, as I say, our 13 group was not allowed to do anything. We could just listen to 14 the proposal and propose something, but we were not in charge. 15 We could not say, "OK, it is going to be implemented" because 16 there was a very strict group of people in Kozarac, people with 17 criminal records, such as Suljo Kusuran who had a group of 18 people under weapons. That was this Cirkin person, I do not 19 know his name, but he was in Kozarusa, who also had a criminal 20 record. They just organised some groups themselves and they 21 were doing everything they pleased. So that created an image of 22 Kozarac. Well, whether the official authorities of Kozarac 23 could prevent such kind of organising of people, that was a 24 question. I remember that they were saying that some 20 26 policemen were ready to sign loyalty, but when those 27 paramilitary groups heard about that, they said, "If you sign 28 loyalty, you would be liquidated, you and your families". So 1 that was some sort of capitulation at that time. There were 2 always some individuals who exacerbated the situation and which 3 we had all found ourselves. There was a group of people in Prijedor a group headed 5 by Duca Knezevic. There was a group in Omarska. They 6 communicated among themselves. It was some sort of competition 7 which went to the expense of the man in the street.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that period from 20th May, the second meeting that took place 9 in Prijedor, and 24th May, the day of the attack on Kozarac, was 10 there any opportunity for the representatives from the civic 11 forum to report back to the Citizens Assembly in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that the civic -- the last Citizens Assembly in 13 Kozarac was held on 21st May '92. We had previously agreed in 14 Prijedor that the Assembly would be attended by a representative 15 from the Crisis Staff, and we were told that Simo Miskovic would 16 attend the Assembly together with Dragan Savanovic, who was at 17 that time Vice President of the municipality and Deputy 18 Commander of the municipal Crisis Staff. They attended the Assembly and I was not present at 20 the meeting. I did not want to be with them because I thought 21 that people would identify me with them, and I think that they 22 were not honest in front of those people. Although Simo 23 Miskovic was trusted by the people in Kozarac because his father 24 used to work as a policeman in Kozarac, he lived there for a 25 very long period of his life and he knew many people in 26 Kozarac. I know he knew Sefik Arnautovic, who was a prominent, 27 respectable citizen in Kozarac. So people trusted him. People 28 believed that he would do something, but I think that he himself 1 was not in the position to do anything special, because he had 2 the Commander of the municipal Crisis Staff behind him and all 3 the military leadership. I know that that meeting was held, but, later on people 5 described to me what had been happening there. There were some 6 disagreements and there was a verbal conflict. I do not know 7 what was being suggested by the representative of the Crisis 8 Staff, but at that time all relations with the Crisis Staff in 9 Prijedor were severed. I remember that, and my neighbours told 10 me, that the same Major Mirsad appeared and he said, "I would 11 rather kill myself than be forced to sign any kind of loyalty to 12 Prijedor. That would be a total capitulation". So they created 13 an unhealthy atmosphere. So they voted that the weapons would not be given 15 back, that the loyalty would not be signed, and the police of 16 Kozarac had previously indicated that if the citizens of Kozarac 17 should decide so, they would sign loyalty. But, as I say, under 18 the pressure of those extremists, that did not happen. So all 19 we could do was try to organise a meeting in Banja Luka. We did 20 have a meeting. I talked with Susic again and with Balic and we 21 had the intention of going to Banja Luka, but it was all too 22 late.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ultimatum that was eventually delivered to Kozarac was the, an 24 ultimatum with a deadline of noon on 24th May 1992. Were you 25 aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. I do not know whether there was exact time very strict 27 ultimatum. Maybe it had been issued, but I do not know. The 28 meetings which we attended were also attended by the 1 representatives of the military in Prijedor and the police. But 2 there was a general chaos at that time. I did not know who the 3 persons in charge were, who members of the Crisis Staff were. Anyway, we were not aware of that ultimatum. That is 5 why we thought, that’s why we wanted to go to Banja Luka, to 6 try and ask for mercy from the President of the security 7 services centre. So there was an attempt. There was an 8 ultimatum, but it was not the last one because the municipal 9 Crisis Staff would always come up with some new conditions. So 10 I don’t think that we would have achieved anything, and the 11 conflict -- the new problems were being created every day. I remember there was a very serious incident in 13 Kozarac on 22nd May. My neighbours told me, "Switch off your 14 lights, there would be shelling", and when I came out of my 15 house I saw people in shelters, and women and children were in 16 shelters and I saw some people in uniform. All of a sudden, 17 I realised how many people were carrying weapons and people whom 18 I had never seen before with weapons carried arms. I was quite 19 shocked to see all that. I was not afraid personally of my neighbours, but 21 among those people in uniform there were many people with 22 criminal records, people who had spent 10 or 15 years in prison, 23 so there was a big risk. So that night, around 10 o'clock, 24 I remember that Suljo Kusuran's group of people seized weapons 25 from two JNA soldiers on the road to Prijedor/Banja Luka. My 26 neighbours told me later on, Adil and Meho Beslagic, that they 27 had seized one sniper and one automatic rifle. Those people went on to Prijedor and they informed 1 their superiors, and that evening there was an order to give 2 back the weapons otherwise Kozarac would be shelled. I was told 3 that by Fikret who was standing in front of my cafe. His cousin 4 told me that we should switch off the lights and that within the next 5 25 minutes something could happen. And I remember there was a black out. There was no public 7 lighting, but I had no place to go. I did not know where 8 I should go because, from some previous conversations with my 9 neighbours, I saw that there was a list of shelters and my name 10 was not there. My family was not on that list, and I did not 11 know what could happen if there really is a shelling. So, in view of such circumstances, I did what I was 13 told to do. I was standing in front of the cafe with Fikret and 14 many people were hiding in shelters. There were vehicles 15 passing by, vehicles that I had never seen before, camouflage 16 colours, along Marsala Tita Street. There was no normal traffic 17 any longer. People were carrying weapons, a lot of people. 18 I do not remember seeing any civilian except for those who were 19 in shelters. I remember I took a bottle of spirits to those 20 people because I knew those shelters. I used to play there as a 21 child.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, but that evening I said to myself, "I should leave, 24 I should flee this town", because I realised that evening in 25 case there is a conflict, I would stand no chance. I would have 26 no chance to flee. So that evening I stayed in a cafe of my 27 neighbour until midnight, with my neighbour Jakupovic, and then 28 I went back home and that evening I slept in my cafe on a chair. I actually slept on the floor and I fell asleep. I do not remember whether I was really sleeping or not. Anyhow, that is how. Morning came and I did not know what had happened, but I heard that everything had been taken care of, and weapons that had caused the incident had been returned. But you never know, you never know whether something similar could happen once again. It was in the air. It was difficult to understand that such an incident over two rifles could bring about a war. But, anyhow, that evening I realised that it was possible. 11 Q. Did you decide then to leave Kozarac? 12 A. Yes, that evening. 13 Q. When did you leave Kozarac? 14 A. That evening I knew I should leave as soon as possible. I did not know when. The next morning when I saw that Relja Trivic's family was packing -- sorry, Trivo Reljic, Reljic Trivo is the man's name -- his family was packing and leaving Kozarac and I asked whether I could go with them and he said, "OK". I did not know what kind of situation was on the road Prijedor/Banja Luka, but after that incident there was a big question whether I could leave Kozarac at all. I spent the whole night thinking how I should leave the town, whether on foot. Then when I saw them packing, I thought that I could perhaps go with them. I did not have a car at that time. I did not have any friends in Kozarac who were not Muslims. 26 Q. Was it only you living in the Tadic family home at that time? 27 A. Yes, I was alone. Well, for a long period of time I had changed the place I slept. When I came back to Kozarac it was -- it was difficult. I slept in my brother's part of the house. Sometimes I would sleep in our family house and sometimes I slept in the garage. I kept changing that because I was afraid. I was afraid that something might happen to me while I am asleep. 6 Q. Who else was in Trivo Reljic's car when you decided to leave Kozarac with him? 8 A. I agreed with him that we should meet in front of the house. It was just opposite my house. He was with his wife and his two sons. Before we left, I just took the register plates from my house. I am afraid that a similar thing might happen when we tried to leave Kozarac with the priest on 3rd May. That is why I suggested to him that I should go on foot and I did not want him to have the same problem. So, I set on along the Marsala Tita Street. I went that part of the road on foot because there were checkpoints there, military checkpoints, of the army from Kozarac. But I passed them and nobody told me anything. I waited for them on the main Banja Luka/Prijedor road and they arrived in their car, zastava 750, and they then took me in their car. I know that before they arrived, an active policeman, Zijad Basic, left in his car. It was also a zastava one, a green zastava. He was living in Kozarac but he was working in Prijedor. 25 Q. So what time was this then that you left your house and went down Marsala Tita Street? 27 A. I remember next to my house, the part which has been shown here several times, there is a restaurant and next to the restaurant there are several shops and several shops are across the street. I remember at that moment in the morning shops were being opened, so it could have been half past 8, 9 o'clock. I saw Mirka Kesic who was opening her shop and I also remember seeing Nasiha -- I think her family name is Susic -- and she was just opening a shoe shop. So it could have been around 8 o'clock in the morning. 8 Q. You referred to taking a register. What do you mean by that, what is that? 10 A. Well, it is actually cashier from my cafe, and it was also a book like a ledger where you would enter all records of beverages and so. They have similar things in shops and it was used in my cafe. All other things that I had were quite too big, like a coffee machine or TV set, but it was all very heavy to carry. I did have some games, but they were all heavy to carry. So it was a very expensive thing and I remembered it so I took it with me. 18 Q. When you moved from the house and you went down to the highway, did Trivo Reljic pick you up in his car? 20 A. Yes, he did. 21 Q. Who else was in that car? 22 A. His wife, his two sons and he. I know we were crammed in the car, but we left. I remember that before we left I had left my jacket because I did not want to leave the impression with the people who were on the road, the soldiers, that I was actually leaving Kozarac. So I took off my jacket and I only had a t-shirt on. It was a bright summer day. I was afraid that something would happen, something that I had felt previously, that I would be prevented from leaving. 2 Q. You referred to the checkpoint in Kozarac that you wanted to get through. Was that between your house and the new Banja Luka/Prijedor highway? 5 A. Yes. That checkpoint was in existence for a very long period of time. It was next to the veterinarian station and it was on the main road, not far from the Jela factory in Kozarac. But at that time when I arrived it was moved closer to the centre of Kozarac. 10 Q. Just so that we have this clear, was that before you actually get on to the highway itself? So if you turned off the highway and went into the main road in the direction of Marsala Tita Street, was the checkpoint in that section of road off the main highway? 15 A. I will try to describe it. 16 Q. If you could just identify it briefly? 17 A. Well, if you go along Marsala Tita Street in the direction of the main road, Prijedor/Banja Luka, the only street after you have passed my house that turns left in the direction of the church, so from that turn some 100 metres on the left there was a checkpoint with soldiers carrying weapons. 22 MR. KAY: Thank you very much. Your Honour, that is a convenient moment. 24 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes. 25 (11.30 a.m.)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 27 (11.50 a.m.) 28 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: Mr. Kay, you may continue. 1 MR. KAY: Thank you, your Honour. 2 Q. Mr. Tadic, can you remember to speak a little bit slower because the interpreters, I must stress, have to listen exactly to what you say and think in two languages and report it to us. So can you remember that, to speak slower? Perhaps if I go like that and move my hand, that is an indication to speak a little bit slower. Thank you. 8 A. I will try. 9 Q. Where did the car of Trivo Reljic then pick you up after you had left Kozarac? 11 A. Around 8 o'clock in the morning. As I said, around the period of time when the stores were opening in Kozarac. 13 Q. I actually asked when. 14 A. On May 23rd 1992. 15 Q. The car that picked you up, which direction did it travel in? 16 A. We were moving out of Kozarac in the direction of Prijedor. 17 Q. Was that on the new highway or the old highway? 18 A. Yes, we were moving along the new highway Prijedor/Banja Luka. 19 Q. Were you stopped during the course of that journey? 20 A. We slowed down twice on the highway. The first time we thought that we would be stopped on the same road near the village of Koncari. That is where was that well-known Suljo Kusuran, "Kole", and he had stopped a military vehicle there and was controlling the documents. We used that moment and just sped up past that. The second time we slowed down at the checkpoint in Orlovci. We did not quite come to stop, but we slowed down and then we went on. I remember at the checkpoint Orlovci I saw there was a lot of military, and I recognised somebody I knew from before. There was Bogoljub Kovac. I think he had a moustache, I remember. 4 Q. The first place that you told us about involving slowing down where Kusuran, otherwise known as "Kole" was, how far from the point where you enter the new road from Kozarac was that first place? 8 A. As you go from Kozarac to the new highway? 9 Q. Yes. 10 A. Somewhere -- I think there is about six kilometres distance. 11 Q. When you went through ---- 12 A. Six kilometres from Kozarac and about one kilometre, maybe two, to Orlovci. I think it is the last village with the Serb majority population, Koncari, as you move towards Kozarac from Prijedor. 16 Q. Did you arrive in Prijedor? 17 A. Yes, that highway Prijedor/Banja Luka goes on to Bosanski Novi and on the same road, a couple of kilometres, and Reljic Trivo with his family stopped off so that I could get off. 20 Q. Where did you get off the car? 21 A. It was on the same road Prijedor/Bosanski Novi across from the railroad station and next to a store, I think it was the "Autoparts", the store that sells that, and I got off there, and they went on to the village of Svodna. 25 Q. What time was that? 26 A. I do not know how much time elapsed, somewhere, 8.00, 8.30, in Kozarac. It could have been 9.30. We were moving fairly slowly because it was an old vehicle and I do not know how much Trivo was using it, not much, some -- because of the fuel. I do not know if you know how zastava 750 looks like. It is a very small car and maybe it was 20 years old. 4 Q. Where did you go in Prijedor? 5 A. On that part of the road there is an unofficial railroad crossing, so I crossed it and I went into the street. I think the name of the street was Preradovica, I am not sure, but I went straight to Jelena Gajic who is my wife's sister. 9 Q. Was she at home or at her place of work that you saw her? 10 A. No, she was at home, both she and the children, also the mother of her husband was there and there were some neighbours. So there were a lot of people there. 13 Q. Did you stay there long? 14 A. Well, I stayed quite a while. I had a coffee. I had something to eat. I did not have time in Kozarac, so I was a bit hungry. 16 Q. What had happened to the cash register? 17 A. The cash register was small but pretty heavy, so I could not carry it, so it went with Trivo. I went in August of '93, so Trivo was keeping it in this village, Svodno, so later he gave it back to me. 21 Q. You said that you stayed at Jelena Gajic's place for quite a while. Did there come a time when you left her place where she lived? 24 A. They told me that there was a train to Banja Luka leaving around 12.00, so I went there. I told them about the circumstances of my leaving Kozarac. I managed to escape and that I was going to my family in Banja Luka. 28 Q. Did you go down to the railway station and catch that train at 1 Prijedor station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the train was already there and it was fairly full. There 3 were people that I knew from before. They were people from 4 Kozarac, from Prijedor. It was packed to capacity. Everybody 5 was wondering if it was going to get going at all. Then around 6 12.00 we heard shells, so we were wondering whether it was going 7 to get going. You could sense those shells flying over the 8 city. The train started after 12.00, and we were all 10 apprehensive, all the way through to Banja Luka, whether it 11 would stop somewhere, it would arrive there, but we all made it 12 to Banja Luka. I remember along the road it was a strange 13 feeling. The tracks were going past the Serb and Muslim 14 villages, but at the end when we got to Banja Luka we had a 15 complete picture of what was going on behind us and it is 16 something that stays in memory. As we were passing, for instance, through Trnopolje, 18 I saw around crowds, people who were alongside the tracks with 19 machine guns, with guns, and then you saw that they had the 20 insignia of the Muslim army, of the Bosnian Army, and the same 21 picture, the same script was in Serb villages, people lying 22 around facing each other and facing the tracks, so that you 23 could see the relationships that were going on at the time. In 24 Ivanjska, that is where the Croats make a majority, they had 25 different insignia, so everybody was armed. So on the train 26 I saw different nationalities. So I think that most people around me felt like me. 28 It did not matter which army would stop you, Serb or Muslim or Croat, and unload us. The train travelled very slowly. Finally, we got there. We stopped and alighted once, and we were thinking, we would wondering. There was a fear among people. The people were not talking much. 5 Q. At what time did the train arrive in Banja Luka? 6 A. Somewhere around 2.00 o'clock in the afternoon. 7 Q. On its way had it stopped at other stations between Prijedor and Banja Luka? 9 A. Yes, the train would stop regularly, but once there were stop lights and it stopped but it would -- there were stations, Petrov Gaj, Trnopolje, Omarska, Ivanjska and Banja Luka. I think those are all the stations where the train stopped. 13 Q. When you arrived in Banja Luka where did you go? 14 A. I only remember that at the exit I greeted Esad Tadzic who is a school friend of my brother. He used to be the President of the municipality in Prijedor. So he was with his wife. We greeted each other. We knew each other well. The families knew each other from before. We just shook hands. We said nothing that is interesting. There was silence, some apprehension and a very strange feeling. He grew up in Kozarac and lived in Prijedor, and I was born and grew up in Kozarac and we both ended up in Banja Luka. I assumed also that he had fled. 23 Q. So where did you go in Banja Luka? 24 A. I went on foot to Starcevica settlement. I came to my brother and told him that I was alive, that I had just arrived from Prijedor and then I went to my family which lived in Koste Jarica Street. 28 Q. What time did you arrive at the place where you were staying in Koste Jarica Street? 2 A. That was in the late afternoon. 3 Q. Having arrived there, did you stay there or did you go anywhere else? 5 A. I stayed there very briefly. I had a strange feeling and I thought that I had to go somewhere. There were several reasons for it. First, I wanted to take a bath. I wanted to eat. I wanted to relax and it was not possible in that house. It had almost nothing there. The food supplies and the money that my wife and my mother had was all spent during their period in Banja Luka. So the relationships were breaking down between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Yugoslavia, and my mother was getting the pension from Belgrade and it stopped and so she had nothing left. They were without money. They had nothing. I had the daily intake from the cafe and that was it. So I suggested, I remembered my friend,[redacted], and we went there. I wanted to have a good meal and I knew that they were rich and I wanted to take a bath, so we went there. 19 Q. You say that you wanted to go there. How far away from the place where you were in Koste Jarica was the place where [redacted] lived? 22 A. It was quite a while, quite a distance, five or six kilometres, the other side of town. It is a family house. It is on a transit road of a completely different part of town. 25 Q. Did you go there with the rest of your family? 26 A. Yes, the whole family came along and we went on foot. 27 Q. So that would be your mother Staka, the two children and your wife Mira? 1 A. Mother Staka, Mira and two children, yes. 2 Q. What time did you get to the [redacted] house? 3 A. It took a while and we carried the younger daughter between us. She was three years then and my mother was not well. She had gangrene on her toe. So it was almost dusk when we arrived. It was already the evening. 7 Q. Who was at the [redacted] house? 8 A. [redacted] [redacted] In other words, the family was there. Only he was living in one part of the house and in another one his brother with wife and mother lived in the other side. He only lived with his wife and daughter. 13 Q. So how long did you stay in this house? 14 A. I was not sure whether I was going to spend the night there. I was not thinking about it. I was not sure that he was going to keep me there. I did not know what was going to happen in the meantime, but [redacted] remained as he was before. So we spent the night and we left only the next evening, towards the evening. 20 Q. Was the house that they were living in a change from the place that you and your family were staying in in Koste Jarica Street? 22 A. It was an exceptional house, very well appointed. The family [redacted] did not have money in the bank, but all the money that they were making, both he and his father, was invested into the house. [Redacted] [Redacted] So, they were quite well off. [Redacted]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 1 Q. The next day is 24th May 1992. At what time did you leave that house? 3 A. Sometime in the afternoon, late afternoon. 4 Q. Where did you go? 5 A. We went to our house where we were living in Koste Jarica Street. That was our reality, so we went back there. 7 Q. The rest of that day, where did you spend that? 8 A. I spent with my family thinking about what to do next. I tried -- I wanted my family to spend as little time there as possible because the conditions were terrible. So we were sitting in front of the house. There was always stench so you could never clean out that inside. There were some old things. I remember that for days and days we cleaned, and you just could not clean it out. So we were sitting in front of the house. Then I installed the antennae so that we had some conditions for living. We were planning what to do next and I said, "We will visit with friends, we will eat there, we will sleep here". We will try to find a job for my wife. That was the short term plan that we had. Other things we did not think about at the time. 22 Q. 24th May was the day that Kozarac was attacked. During the next five days did you go into Kozarac? Did you return to Kozarac at all? 25 A. During the conflict in the Kozarac area, I did not go. The first information I heard on radio and television. I remember well that after about four or five days TV Banja Luka showed what was going on precisely in or around Kozarac. I remember Kotlovaca -- that is on Mount Kozara -- and they were showing -- that was where people went. They said that they -- the extremists burnt down a mountain lodge. Those were the first information -- that was the first information I saw on television. So, in a way I was following the news, mostly through television. They had their own view of events and I had left that town a few days ago, but the television had its own version of the truth. I remember well that they said that there was an agreement of sorts between the Crisis Staff and the Local Commune of Kozarac, that there was an agreement -- that there was an agreement between the two authorities that the buses would be sent to Kozarac by the authorities in Prijedor to take out civilians and that this was all part of the agreement between the Crisis Staff and the Local Commune authorities. 16 Q. When did you first return to Kozarac, having left it on 23rd May? 18 A. I think it was 1st June 1992. 19 Q. I want to ask you about that period between those two dates of 23rd May and 1st June. How did you spend your time? 21 A. I spent my time with the family. For the most part, we cleaned the house. You just could not clean it out. That was one thing. On the other hand, in agreement with Jovo Samardzija, who was getting his pension in Banja Luka, I wanted to see that my mother was also receiving it there. She was registered in Prijedor municipality, so because she suddenly left the municipality she was cut off. So I went to the veterans' organisation. I had to 1 open a bank account, and then had it forwarded to Belgrade. 2 I registered my family with the Red Cross in Banja Luka. Then 3 they were surprised how come there was a refugee from the 4 Prijedor municipality. After an interview with the 5 administrative worker at the Red Cross there, he said, "Yes, 6 I will put you in with the refugees from Livno because so far 7 nobody has reported from the Prijedor region. You are the first 8 one". So we finally got a status. So that is the business that I finished until 10 1st June. Then we were visiting our friends. We visited with 11 Nikola Petrovic, a long time friend. I have known him since the 12 secondary school. He was going out with my wife's friend who 13 was also a nurse. So we knew each other through those 14 contacts. Also, he was an athlete, so we also met while we were 15 training together. So we went there. We had lunch with him. After that we visited my uncle, Risto Vokic. 17 I visited him primarily because we said that we were trying to 18 find a job for my wife as a nurse in a hospital. He had some 19 influence in Banja Luka. He said that he would see. We were 20 all at his place and I remember he returned us in his car 21 to Starcevica. He was at the time driving a zastava 101 model. So then we were dealing with trying to fix the house 23 and visit with old friends, and pretty much on a daily basis 24 I would go, if I went to my brother's, who had a business in the 25 same settlement, Starcevica, in Milosa Duica Street, and then we 26 would also often go to Jovo Samardzija. He was a long time 27 friend of my father's and we would go there to have coffee and 28 that kind of thing. Almost every night I was spending in my brother's company. At that time they were securing that area, that one part of that street and then another part, and I remember that on one occasion they did a silly thing. They put some tree trunks there and some policeman ran into it with his car, and so they were criticised. They were civilian defence. 7 Q. You referred there to a brother, which brother is that? 8 A. I mean Ljubomir. 9 Q. 1st June then is the first day that you returned to Kozarac. Did you go with anyone or were you by yourself? 11 A. From the moment when myself and my brother heard that the war operation in Kozarac area had stopped and you could find that out through the radio and newspapers, they said that the conflict was over, that the extremists had surrendered. In other words, they made it known that there was peace in the area, and my brother insisted that we go there. He had a store there and he had had a delivery of goods right before the war and that cost a lot of money. I was not eager. I was, kind of, disappointed but he always insisted day after day. 20 Q. Would that be your brother Ljubomir again? 21 A. Yes, at that time, for the most part, I spent time with him. He was living about a kilometre away and he was spending the time in that street, Milosa Duica, where I lived. He had his business there because he was living at his mother-in-law's and that was really an emergency residence, and he was spending time at his wife's place where she was with her children. 27 Q. How did you travel to Kozarac then on 1st June? 28 A. We took a train. 1 Q. What time did you leave? 2 A. We went in the morning. I cannot recall, but they were running often, frequently, around 5.00 and 6.00, and I think that that was the only means of transportation that was used at the time. 5 Q. Which station did you go to? 6 A. We first arrived in Omarska, the town of Omarska. Then we did not know what circumstances are, what the conditions are, in the area. We asked people and there were a lot of people wearing arms in the area. Mostly, people were talking about the events, that it was the war had started. Then we were asking around, what was the way to Kozarac? I did not know too many people in Omarska because there was never much communication between Omarska and Kozarac. 14 Q. What was the reason for going to Omarska railway station? 15 A. There was no other way. The train stopped in Omarska and there was no other way to get to Kozarac. That was the only way. My brother had a car, but it was very risky to use it. It was a Ford which he had bought in Germany and there was always something amiss with it. 20 Q. We have heard that the railway station for Kozarac town is, in fact, at Trnopolje? Was there any reason why you did not go on the train to Trnopolje? 23 A. Yes, it was not possible to go from Trnopolje to Kozarac. You would have had to walk for six kilometres. That was the only reason. In other words, it was much farther. 26 Q. Going to Omarska then, what time did you get off the train? 27 A. Somewhere maybe around noon we got to Omarska. Then we asked around what the conditions were, how we could get to the centre of Kozarac? Then some people pointed us in some kind of a headquarters, and we asked whether we could go to the place where we lived. They said it was not their authority; it was a regional Crisis Staff in Omarska. They called it headquarters or staff. It was really a one room where a uniformed officer was sitting and he said that the Kozarac was -- that in the Lamovita Crisis Staff is where we should find out about Kozarac. So we went there on foot and there, at least, I knew someone. I remember a waiter, Nenad Rakic, and I asked him, "Is there war in Kozarac?" He said, "No, no, it is all over, there are almost no people left". I was surprised, "How come?" He said, "Well, they were all evacuated". Then my brother and I went to the village, Timarci or Babici, I do not know what the official name is. That is where my waiter lived, Milenko Timarac. 17 Q. You said that this would have come under the Lamovita Crisis Staff. Where was that situated? 19 A. It was in a Local Commune there. Previously -- I think it was the first time that I saw -- I visited a Local Commune there. It was like a youth centre there and they said, "This is where the regional Crisis Staff is which has authority over Kozarac. It is all -- Kozarac is part of that". I do not know. It was exclusively a military formation. I remember that there was a municipal Crisis Staff and then some people explained that now they had the absolute authority there. 27 Q. Did you see Milenko Timarac? 28 A. Yes, we went to Timarac, to his house. We asked him, we said that we wanted to visit the house. He knew that I had a cafe, but he used to work there as a waiter but not the last six months. He agreed, and he said, "But you need a permit. You have to get a certificate for fuel", and then we agreed that I would look for that. So we went back to Lamovita. I went to the Local Commune because my brother was not officially registered there. I had a personal ID. I told them that I lived in Kozarac, and I told them that I am going to request them to go to Kozarac to visit my family house. 10 Q. When you went to Lamovita and first of all saw Milenko Timarac, about what time was this? 12 A. Well, it was all around -- between 12.00 and 1.00 p.m. 13 Q. When you went to the local Crisis Staff at Lamovita, what time would that have been? 15 A. Well, right after that we did that relatively fast. The village of Timarac is very close to Lamovita. It was all very quickly maybe. We left around 2 o'clock for Kozarac, not later than that. 19 Q. What vehicle did Milenko Timarac have? 20 A. Milenko had a zastava 101, white in colour. It was in a bad state of repair, but it served the purpose. 22 Q. Is that a saloon car? 23 A. No, it is a luxury car. I know that he used to live in Sisak, in Croatia, before the war, so he never changed his plates. It was always on his car. 26 Q. In that car were you able to travel into Kozarac? 27 A. Yes, first we got the permit, I mean the certificate for the fuel. It was recorded somewhere and I know that the Secretary of the Local Commune, Drago Milencic issued me that. I met other people there and they told me that the Commander of the Crisis Staff there was Vinko Kos and he issued approval for me to get the fuel. So we went to the petrol station in Lamovita. We got the fuel and we went to Kozarac. We took the old Prijedor/Banja Luka road. 7 Q. When you entered Kozarac were you able to pass into it without difficulty or were you stopped on the way? 9 A. There was a spot where they had some kind of control, unofficial control. It was in the direction of Kozarac when you leave Lamovita, but we stopped somewhere along the road and two more passengers joined us, Boza and Mirko Grahovac whom we knew from Kozarac. They were coming from the village of Lukici. They were also going to Kozarac on foot. So we gave them a lift and we arrived in Kozarac together. 16 Q. You said that you were stopped at a point. Who was running that point? Who controlled that point? 18 A. Well, honestly, I do not know. It was a person in uniform, half uniform, half civilian clothes. He had an M48 rifle and there were some other villagers standing with him. They were not really organised and there was an obstacle on the road, a tree trunk. That is why I am saying it was an unofficial checkpoint. They did not know what they really wanted when they stopped us. They did not ask us anything. They just asked us where we were going. I told them that we were going to Kozarac and they said, "OK, you can go to Kozarac". 27 Q. Did you visit the family home on this occasion of 1st June? 28 A. Yes, I did. Before I visited the house on the road next to the church where there used to be a checkpoint Grahovac and his wife got out, and they went to their family house and we went to the centre of the town to our family house. 4 Q. At what time did you get to the Tadic family house? 5 A. Well, it could have been about 3.00 o'clock, 3.00 p.m. I know that we had been, that we were travelling for about one hour, hour and a half. We just drove through Kozarac, the three of us. We went to -- I remember we went in the direction of the fire station. Then we went back when we saw what was happening there, what had happened there, that a lot of it had been destroyed. So we went back to the factory, Jela factory, and that is where I saw an acquaintance of mine. It all lasted very short because when we went back Kozarac was in a pitiful shape. It was not so much destroyed, but there was a stench in the air. There was no electricity at that time. So later on in my house I saw in my freezer that all the food that I had had been spoiled, there was some cattle around. It was difficult to explain such a feeling, but you could feel something in the air, you could feel that something was unhealthy in the air. We did not see many soldiers. I saw several people, that was all. All along the road I just saw that unofficial control near Lamovita and later I did not see anyone when we were going there or when we were coming back. 24 Q. For how long did you stay in the area of Kozarac on this visit? 25 A. Well, one hour, an hour and a half. We wanted to do something useful. My brother wanted to do something about his business premises. He wanted to protect something. I tried to shut down the area because everything was laying open and things were scattered around. So I first established the situation. So during that first visit to our family house we realised that the house had not been really destroyed but the front part of the house where there were business premises of my brother, there was a huge opening, a huge hole of maybe a shell. The part of the house where I had been sleeping for several months, that is the part of the house that belongs to my brother Mladen, there was a hole in the roof which had been made by a shell, and a shell had fallen in front of the house and damaged the terrace. So it was quite a pitiful shape. My cafe was damaged. Everything was more or less damaged. It was a rather sophisticated kind of interior in the cafe. So when windows were smashed and doors were smashed, everything was just laying open. The town itself was ghostly. 15 Q. Had anything been removed from either your house or your cafe premises or Ljubo's business premises so far as you could tell on this visit? 18 A. Not at that time. Well, I did not check details. I did not really think about that. I just saw that most of the valuable equipment in my cafe was OK. So that the coffee machine was damaged, but it was still usable. The TV set was still there because I had two TV sets, one in my house where I was living and the other in the cafe, in my business premises. I had two games machines. Most of it was OK. The property had been damaged, but it was still usable. 26 Q. Did you take anything with you from the house when you left it after this visit? 28 A. I took only, as far as I can recall, my stereo chain, the one I was using in my cafe. It is very expensive equipment. I spent DM4,500 on that. So I thought I should take that. I put it in Milenko's car although he protested, but I could not take anything else except for that. It did not take up too much space. 6 Q. A stereo chain, what is that? 7 A. Well, that is it, that is a musical equipment stereo system without musical boxes, without loud speakers, they were too big to carry. I remember I left that with Milenko Timarac in his house and that equipment stayed in his house for quite a while. I do not remember when I took it to my family house. 12 Q. When did you arrive at Milenko Timarac's house? What time was that? 14 A. Late in the afternoon, very late. I do not recall what time it was, but I know we did not stay too long in Kozarac. There was an incident in the street with my brother and it was quite unsafe. We were there as civilians. Milenko warned us, he told us that we should not stay there too long. Then it was not difficult when you were wearing civilian clothes, if people see you wearing civilian clothes. There was a chaos in the street at that time. There were very old men in uniforms, men aged 75 and young men as young as 18. The situation was rather awkward and as a civilian it was not wise to walk around the street. My brother had a kind of incident at that time, and the person warned us. He told us it was still an area under military operations. I forgot to say that in addition to the cash register, I took my hunting rifle and my other rifle from the house, after the warning of this officer who told us it was quite risky to move around. Before that incident we did not have any weapons with us. 3 Q. You referred then to the cash register. As I understood your evidence, you told us that the cash register was taken when you left Kozarac on 23rd May? 6 A. Yes. 7 Q. The weapons that you have referred to, did you take them on the 23rd May or the visit on 1st June? 9 A. On 1st June. On 23rd May I did not have any weapons with me. Even the handgun that I had for which I had a permit was not there. I had left it with my wife in Banja Luka because during her stay in Banja Luka the place was attacked two times. A window was smashed and they wanted to rob the house. So once after I had left the gun with my wife, she was keeping the gun although she could not really handle it, she was not strong enough. So I left it with her. 17 Q. I would like to ask you now about weapons. What weapons did you own at this time? 19 A. Well, after 1985 I filed a request, an application, and I was allowed and consequently I bought a gun, a 765, zastava make, and I kept it at home mostly. Except for that weapon, my brother who had spent the last four months of 1991, my brother Mladen, he stayed in Kozarac quite a few times. He had some problems with his wife in Munich. So he tried to come back and live in Kozarac. That was his idea. He was in the process of building his business premises, so he would spend a long time in Kozarac with his daughter. Because he was a hunter he brought a hunting rifle and that hunting rifle was always in the house. He was the owner of the hunting rifle. At the end of 1991 I got an automatic rifle from a deserter whose name was Mile Kusota. 3 Q. The hunting rifle that you referred to then which belonged to Mladen, did you take that from the house on 1st June? 5 A. Yes, I did take it with me, but it was useless. It used to be a very expensive rifle. He had bought it in Munich. It cost him between DM6,000 and DM7,000. It had some decoration on it as far as I can remember. So I took it, although I could not really use it. You could take it apart, so it was quite safe. Children could not use it. Even adults who did not know how to use it could not really use if they did not have the mechanism which I kept always apart. It was not in my house, but when my brothers were not in Kozarac I was using their parts of the house and I was keeping an eye on it. So his rifle was always there in his part of the house. So I took apart that mechanism, firing mechanism, from the rest of the rifle and I could not find that mechanism. It had disappeared. Someone had taken it away. I think that it was gold plated, that mechanism. 19 Q. The automatic rifle you told us about that you had got at the end of 1991, did you take that away on 1st June? 21 A. Yes, I did. 22 Q. Did you take both of those weapons to Lamovita with you? 23 A. Well, first we went to Milenko's house where I left the hunting rifle because it could not be used anyway, and I took the automatic rifle with me to Banja Luka. 26 Q. What time then did you leave Lamovita to continue your journey to Banja Luka? 28 A. Well, we did not go to Lamovita. I do not know whether I mentioned that. Milenko, from his house there are two roads. The village of Timaraci is between the road, the main Banja Luka/Prijedor road and the old Prijedor/Banja Luka road, somewhere in the vicinity of the village of Jakupovici. So there are several roads that you can take if you want to go to the main Prijedor/Banja Luka road from that village. So he took us along a village road, a village street, which joins the main road somewhere after Kamicani. So he took us there and he took us in his car to the junction Lamovita/Omarska road and Prijedor/Banja Luka road. There is a junction there and there is a petrol station there on the right-hand side, and that is where we waited for about 15 minutes. So after we arrived in the village of Timaraci we did not go back to Lamovita. That is what we did when we were coming to Kozarac. 15 Q. So where did you go having finished your business in Timaraci? 16 A. We hitchhiked a vehicle and went to Banja Luka. I believe it was a lorry.
