I do not want to get bogged down too much in the detail of that as I do not see it as being important. 19 A. But I have to tell you that in paragraph No. 3 which states that the local board of the SDS at that time was verified by the Citizens Assembly, that it had taken over the responsibilities and duties of the Council of the Local Commune of Kozarac, but at that time there was no Council. So the local board of the SDS by a decision of the Assembly of the Local Community took over responsibility of the Council of the local board which was established in October 1992. That is all I wanted to add. 27 Q. Thank you. Let us go to Exhibit 334. If the English can be put on the monitor and the Serbo-Croat in front of the witness. 1 This is a document where we see that the Chairman of the 2 Citizens Assembly that you told us about, Bosko Dragicevic, 3 signed it. It concerns a meeting of 22nd August 1992. It is a 4 decision on the resumption of work of the Kozarac Local 5 Commune. Is it right again that this was part of the procedure 6 that was attempting to start work to revive Kozarac after the 7 impact of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. This document and these decisions here were 9 preceded by some meetings, meetings that were held on 15th 10 August 1992, without what meetings it would have been impossible 11 to reach any kind of decision whatsoever. On the basis of this 12 decision the municipal Crisis Staff in Prijedor could react. 13 They were sent one copy and they were thus forced to revoke the 14 decision, the first decision in relation to the Local Commune in 15 Kozarac, because this decision was based on previous meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did they revoke that decision in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The decision was revoked after we sent this decision, our 18 decision. We had had talks previously in the Prijedor town 19 hall, but after we established the local board of the SDS and 20 after we elected the President of the Council and the President 21 of the Local Commune Assembly, we had a basis, a grounds for our 22 request. Here, and this is the most important of our decisions, 23 it says, "After the war operations in the territory of Kozarac 24 the Kozarac Local Commune resumed its work." That was the result 25 of everything that had happened before. They simply could not 26 do anything against this particular decision. They simply had 27 to alter their previous decision, and by "they" I mean members 28 of the municipal Crisis Staff. 1 Q. If we look now at Exhibit 335 dated 31st August 1992, if the English could be put on the monitor and the Serbo-Croat in front of the defendant. 4 A. I forgot to tell you, you have here the signature of Bosko Dragicevic. You have to ask yourselves why there is no mention of Goran Borovnica here. He was only Chairman at one session until the President of the Local Commune was elected, that was Bosko Dragicevic and he worked as the President of the Assembly until the end of '92. In '93 that was the highest political function within the Local Commune. 11 Q. I think you have made that clear to us, that at the initial meeting someone who was a local figure, and you told us about him being involved in the war, had to take the chair for the meeting and then appointments were made as a result of the elections afterwards. Looking at document 335, we can see here that this is a programme for the local board of the SDS in relation to events within the Local Commune. Again, this date of 31st August 1992, was it important because decisions were able thereafter to be made relating to improvement of the condition of the town of Kozarac? 22 A. Well, this decision was part of decisions, previous decisions which began as of 15th August. It was not maybe done very professionally, because we were never really politically active in relation to the work of the Local Commune. So, this may not be very professional, but we did have a written basis for activities that followed in the Local Commune in Kozarac. On 31st August 1992 not all bodies of the Local Commune in Kozarac 1 functioned. There was a period which preceded the real work of 2 the Local Commune in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit 151, and again if the English could 4 be put on the monitor and the Serbo-Croat in front of the 5 defendant. This is a document dated 9th November 1992, but it 6 refers to the decision on 31st August and refers to the election 7 of the Kozarac Local Commune Secretary on 9th November. Can you 8 tell us about this document which refers to the earlier dates, 9 and in paragraph two refers to the competition of 9th September 10 1992: "Dusko Tadic from Kozarac has been appointed Kozarac Local 11 Commune Secretary"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This decision refers to the decision of 31st August 1992, 13 and relates mainly to the work of the Local Commune. It is 14 impossible for a local commune to function without a secretary 15 of the Local Commune, a fully employed secretary of the Local 16 Commune. A secretary was always a professional position, but it 17 had nothing to do with the party activity, the work of the 18 political parties. I do not know whether you have a decision on 19 the competition. The decision on the appointment was preceded 20 by competition for the position of the secretary to the Local 21 Commune. That competition is mentioned here in paragraph two. 22 So on the basis of the competition of 9th September 1992, Dusko 23 Tadic from Kozarac has been appointed for the Local Commune 24 Secretary. So there had been competition before. Anybody could 25 apply for that position, but I remember that period very well. 26 That competition was open and it was publicly announced in 27 Prijedor on the books, such was the procedure. So it was 28 publicly announced, but nobody applied for it simply because 1 people had no interest whatsoever to go and work in Kozarac in 2 view of its state. I remember I was the only one who showed any interest 4 in taking up that position. So the decision on the appointment 5 of the Kozarac Local Commune Secretary was reached by the 6 Assembly of the Kozarac Local Commune, the very same Assembly. 7 I mean all the citizens, all the residents, of the Kozarac Local 8 Commune. Here you have mention of the President of the Assembly 9 of the Local Commune which was always the highest body in the 10 Local Commune. At that time the President was Bosko Dragicevic, 11 and he was the Chairman at that meeting when I was elected 12 Secretary to the Local Commune. All these decisions relate to the beginning of the 14 work of the Kozarac Local Commune. It was the period of August 15 1992, and during that period there were not many people who were 16 interested in doing anything in Kozarac. In respect to June 17 1992 the time of my first visit, it was already -- it had 18 changed. It was something like we have seen here on video. It 19 was not the same place, the same place I visited the first time 20 I went there. It was systematically destroyed, although it was 21 in the jurisdiction of the municipal Crisis Staff. There were 22 some people who were providing security, but there were also 23 many military formations in Kozarac at that time who were 24 ostensibly protecting the town, but ----

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time were you also involved with the Kozarac local 26 police as well as starting this project of working in Kozarac 27 trying to restore the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from early September 1992, maybe that is why it is unclear 1 in the documents, but it is a procedure when at the beginning of 2 September I became part of the revival of Kozarac and I still 3 had duties with securing the railway and bus station in 4 Prijedor. So that I was often and for the most part in the 5 field all day. So, if I was on duty at the bus station in 6 Prijedor, at say 9.00 o'clock in the evening, so the whole 7 morning I would spend in Kozarac with these assistants and then 8 I would come to duty and then after a while I just could not 9 take it any more. That whole activity started in August and 10 then finally physically I was just not able to do it any more. 11 So that was the reason why I moved from the police, from the 12 Prijedor police to the Kozarac police, because it was not 13 possible to leave the police. Had I left then I would have been 14 mobilized, I would be would have been conscripted. It would not 15 have been possible to interrupt the duties as a policeman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you cease working for the Kozarac local police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stopped working exactly on 19th November 1992. However, the same 18 month though, I think it was on 6th November, I got days off 19 from the Commander of the police station because I was involved 20 in different committees, different commissions, which worked on 21 the revival. It was about markings which is what we saw. There 22 were circles with crosses. The first action that we had was the 23 protection of the structures that were in the centre of 24 Kozarac. The only way to do it legally was to form a municipal 25 commission that was to find out the conditions of the 26 residential fund in Kozarac. Blue, red and white signified 27 the -- and the difference in colours as you may have been able 28 to see -- each colour signified a certain degree of 1 destruction. This work was done by the Municipal Commission 2 from Prijedor, and it was the precondition for any kind of 3 reconstruction of these structures. So that was taking a 4 picture of the conditions of the residential buildings, and this 5 was the first time -- the centre of Kozarac was not destroyed. 6 Maybe there were damages, maybe 20 per cent, but 80 per cent of 7 the damage that ensued happened later in the period between June 8 1992 and the end of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this time which really begins from the middle of August 1992 10 when you are attempting to restore Kozarac and onwards, did you 11 have refugees coming into the area of Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was another reason why we raised our voice against those 13 activities, simply because we were surprised when we saw from 14 the beginning of July 1992, I worked at the checkpoint Orlovci, 15 I saw the refugees coming through. It was true that they had 16 been expelled from their own homes where they used to live 17 before, but it is also true that they could have moved into the 18 centre of Kozarac. I still claim that had those people moved 19 there Kozarac would not have been destroyed. It is true that 20 people who never lived there would have now been living there, 21 but it would not have been destroyed. So the regional Crisis Staff of Trnopolje organised 23 this activity and they moved some people in that area of 24 Trnopolje. As I said, before the regional Crisis Staff had been 25 formed and the one in Trnopolje was covered and overnight they 26 brought a decision that their area comprised from the railroad 27 tracks to the main road to Kozarac, and the centre of Kozarac, 28 which was the most valuable, was now belonging to the regional 1 Crisis Staff in Lamovita who decided that it was not going to be 2 revived. So they never wanted to protect it and they never had 3 any intentions of protecting it. So if you look at Hrnici, Suhi 4 Brod and the other parts there, that is where people live. That 5 is where in July and August people were moved in, organised by 6 the regional Crisis Staff of Trnopolje thinking that it was 7 incumbent upon them to do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because you were Secretary of the Local Commune, did that count 9 as a form of work obligation that meant that you did not have to 10 be mobilized for the military and undertake military duties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the reason which followed out of all these 12 activities. It would not have been possible to work as a 13 Secretary of the Local Commune and continue working in the 14 police. But from the takeover of power in Prijedor and on, 15 I was getting more and more an impression that there was a 16 split, a schism. The SDS had no activity. They stopped 17 their activity and the Crisis Staff took over all activities. 18 Because of the events, the dominant positions were occupied by 19 the military personnel, by officers, and the war zones and the 20 war effort was given the highest priority. Everything else was 21 neglected. As far as the work duties are concerned, I have to say 23 one more thing. One of the reasons maybe why I was not 24 mobilized before June 16th 1992 -- there are several reasons. 25 One of the reasons is that I acted the way I did, in other words 26 I was in Banja Luka. The other one is that 10 years before the 27 I mostly was in private business and at one time even in Banja 28 Luka, and at that time I was tied militarily to my firm, to my company and while I was in Croatia. That is why I was never mobilized for the war in Croatia, in the first place. Also in the former Yugoslavia people who were in private business were almost never mobilized. 5 Q. At one stage you were issued with a certificate which excused you from the military as a result of your position as Secretary of the Local Commune which counted as your work obligation, is that right? 9 A. Yes. That request by the procedure was produced by the Executive Board of the Local Commune in Kozarac, but it had not been acted on. It was not acted on until early 1993. Simply, I was still from 19th November on, I was free of that, but there was always a possibility to be involved in any police activity in Kozarac. But because of this procedure until the end of, up towards the end of 1992 I was already freed of these obligations, so I worked as Secretary for the Local Commune. 17 Q. Can we look at Prosecution Exhibit 154. We see here a document that is -- if the English can be put on the overhead monitor -- the decision on the assignment of work obligations. This document states that your post as Secretary of the Local Commune in Kozarac is to be considered a combat assignment, and if there is a call for mobilization you should report immediately to the post you were assigned to. Were there in fact attempts by the military to mobilize you and put you within the military forces? 26 A. Yes. 27 Q. Although you had an exemption by reason of your work obligation, were the military in fact accepting that as being something that you were able to use to avoid being mobilized within the military? 3 A. Beside this one, on 25th December 1992 I was permanently removed from the list of the reserve police force, and that was always a problem. The cessation of duties towards a unit of any kind was always when you got the final seal in the military booklet. So my first entry, the first seal is on 16th June, and the last day I think is 25th December 1992. My obligation ceased both regarding the military and the police. At that time I was officially fully employed as Secretary for the Local Commune. The procedure that the Assembly made in order for me not to be recalled to the military or the police, was completed with this decision when I was put in the position of Secretary of the Local Commune. Here it says, "conscript". Any person, regardless of whether they were police or the military, had a military obligation. So that where it later says that one should report to a post, according to this decision it says, it is a post to where I should report in the future and that meant from this date on. It meant the position of the Secretary of the Local Commune. So this is my post. That was also my workplace as of that date. 22 Q. Were there attempts by the military to forcibly enlist you for military service? 24 A. Yes. 25 Q. When did those attempts by the military take place? 26 A. Those activities started first in March 1993 and up to August 1993. In other words, half a year I was exposed to the military police in Prijedor. In the first period, from March till June 1992 I was arrested several times by the military police. I would always show them this document. The patrol leaders at that time told me that this is a document which obligated them to release me. So they could not mobilize me without revoking this decision, and this decision could only be revoked by the men in charge of the National Defence. 7 JUDGE STEPHEN: The witness has said March till June 1992. 8 MR. KAY: Your Honour, yes. [To the witness]: Was that right, March till June 1992 you were arrested several times by the police? Is that the right year? 11 A. Yes. 12 Q. 1992? 13 A. 1993, I made a mistake. 14 Q. Thank you. Perhaps if we just slow things down a little bit, Mr. Tadic, which is why I am searching for a document. It is always a useful recourse. Can we have Exhibit D8. 17 A. If I can, I started reading this ---- 18 Q. No. If you can just wait for the document. 19 A. If it was translated this is handwritten. 20 Q. Let us just go to a document here which will tie matters in. If page 15 of the English can be put on the monitor and if you could put this in front of the witness. I would like you to look at section 10. Section 10 of the military book shows your participation in war and it has your mobilization date of 16th June 1992. That date you told us of, 25th December 1992. Did that not release you then from any further obligation, taking into account that decision that you had on the assignment of your work obligations? 1 A. I think that the decision made on the work obligation was made in early '93. 3 Q. Yes. Why then in 1993 were the military forces attempting to mobilize you contrary to your exemption? 5 A. It was absolutely illegal, and it was illegal relative to the laws of Republika Srspka. They could not have mobilized me. It was illegal of them. As far as the stamps are concerned, the first stamp is the security services centre, that is an old stamp of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I know its shape, and the last stamp is the stamp of Republika Srpska, also the police stamp. 11 Q. We also see as part of this section 10 the date of 10th June 1993. Was that a date that you were mobilized at the front by the military? 14 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: You may have to move it. Is it on this Exhibit, Mr. Kay? 16 MR. KAY: Sorry, yes. If you can move it up the screen a bit. I am sorry, your Honour. Thank you. Section two as translated. Is that the date that you were mobilized at the front? 19 A. Yes, and that was the stamp of the military. As I said, it was illegal because on 10th June I had a work obligation as a Secretary of the Local Commune. The real procedure was to revoke that decision by the Ministry of Defence office in Prijedor, and only then could they make decisions about my assignment to the police or the military. So they had no right to do that. I remember that I visited Slavko Budimir on this matter and he said that he could not revoke this decision because I was fully employed as a Secretary of the Local Commune. I was being paid, given a salary, and the Assembly of both Kozarac and Prijedor had to be involved in the process. So he had no answer why they were doing it. 3 Q. Stop there. How many attempts had been made to arrest you before you were mobilized on 10th June 1993? Do not give me the details, just the numbers. 6 A. From March until this date, five or six attempts. Sometimes I jumped out of the window. Sometimes I would take cover from where I was sitting, but there were several attempts in Kozarac to arrest me. Several times the military police came. I would show them the documents. They would not arrest me, but they had an arrest warrant for me. They said, "It is all fine, we have other people, but for some reason they want to arrest you." 13 Q. On 10th June 1993 where were you mobilized to? 14 A. On that date I was arrested in Kozarac at the gas station, and a patrol chief, his name was Desimir, and his colleague, I think his name was Lajic, they took me to Prijedor in a van with another group of people. On the same day transferred me to the war zone near Gradacac. They told me in Kozarac they were taking me in for an information conversation, and I told them that I had a uniform and should I bring it. They said, "No. No, we are just taking you in for an interview" -- Vujicic was his name -- "and you will be released immediately." Their headquarters were in the fire station. I was surprised when I was just given travel documents. They said: "Take him to Gradacac." I said: "What interview in Gradacac?" They said: "Everything is fine. You are going to an interview with the Chief of the Military Security who is near Gradacac and you have to talk to him. He is there so you have to go there." They did not tell me that I would be put in a unit. They just told me there would be an interview, a conversation. 3 Q. Were you taken then to the front at Gradacac? 4 A. Yes. 5 Q. How long did you stay at the front at Gradacac? 6 A. They first took me to the command in Srednja Slatina. I waited for an hour and then that Desimir came out and said: "The Chief of Police is not going to talk to you. We have orders to put you in on the first line of fire." So they took me to that zone, into that zone, and that is where I spent the first night. Nobody gave me a weapon or told me anything, to sign up for anything. So they just brought me there and they left me there. 14 Q. Did you remain serving at Gradacac or did you terminate your duty early? 16 A. The next day I escaped from there. I remember I saw Jozo Popovic there who was also mobilized as a civilian. So I was not the only one, but I did not want to leave it at that. So I met a truck driver who was bringing in food supplies and I asked him if he would help me get out of that there, and he said that he would. So I took a ride with him. I hid in the truck when it was returning. I did not know that area, otherwise I would have left on foot. That was not a problem. 24 Q. Did you desert? 25 A. I did not consider myself a deserter. I left because it was illegal. They considered it desertion. 27 MR. KAY: Your Honour, that is an appropriate moment. 28 THE PRESIDING JUDGE: We will adjourn until tomorrow at 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (The court adjourned until the following day).
